title: Monetary Policy Report - April 2026
summary: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 to maintain Bank Rate at 3.75% at its April 2026 meeting, despite CPI inflation rising to 3.3% in March. The MPC cited the Middle East conflict as causing a sharp rise in global energy prices, which has changed the inflation outlook from three months ago when inflation was expected to approach the 2% target. The Committee judges that monetary policy cannot undo energy price increases but will act to prevent second-round effects from becoming embedded in wage and price-setting behaviour.
key_points: MPC voted 8-1 to maintain Bank Rate at 3.75%; one member preferred a 0.25pp increase to 4%
CPI inflation increased to 3.3% in March and is expected to rise further as energy price effects pass through
Middle East conflict has caused sharp rises in global energy prices, disrupting energy supplies
Monetary policy cannot undo global energy price increases; takes time to work through economy
Labour market continues to loosen with unemployment rising since 2024, which may contain second-round wage effects
MPC will monitor evidence and stands ready to act to ensure CPI inflation returns to 2% target sustainably
why_it_matters: This quarterly report is the primary official document explaining the Bank of England's inflation analysis and rate decisions. The maintenance of rates despite higher inflation reflects the MPC's view that second-round effects remain contained by weak demand, though the Committee acknowledges uncertainty. Market participants need to understand the BoE's two key policy judgements: that labour market weakness limits second-round effects, and that policy must balance the costs of leaning too little against responding too much.
macro_context: The Middle East conflict has created a significant energy price shock that has pushed UK CPI inflation to 3.3%, above the 2% target. The report presents three scenarios illustrating possible outcomes depending on energy price persistence and whether second-round effects materialize. The MPC emphasises that any policy action now cannot prevent near-term inflation rises due to lag effects, but can prevent the shock from becoming embedded in broad-based inflation. Weak demand and loosening labour market provide some offset, but elevated household inflation expectations and companies' heightened price sensitivity post-pandemic represent upside risks to inflation.
